background_notes.fact: The map Jf(x)=-f(-x) is an involution on periodic distributions with Fourier coefficients -hat f(-k). It preserves reality, zero mean and every homogeneous or inhomogeneous Sobolev norm. Multipliers exp(±it k^3) are isometries of these spaces, preserve reality and zero mean, and are strongly continuous in t.

background_notes.justification: Substitution x to -x in the periodic pairing gives the reflection formula. Reindex k to -k in the norm sums. Phases have modulus one and their values at -k are conjugates of their values at k. Strong continuity follows first on finite Fourier sums and then for any datum by controlling the weighted square-summable tail uniformly in t. This also converts source twisted-flow continuity to physical-flow continuity.

background_notes.fact: If U is a C_t L2 real periodic distributional solution of U_t=U U_x+U_xxx, interpreting U U_x=(1/2)partial_x(U^2), then u(t,x)=-U(t,-x) solves u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)partial_x(u^2), and J is an inverse correspondence between these solution classes. It preserves limits in C_t L2 and in Sobolev norms.

background_notes.justification: Let P be spatial reflection. Distributionally u_t=-P U_t, u_xxx=P U_xxx and partial_x(u^2)=-P partial_x(U^2). Substitution in the source equation gives the target identity. Test functions may be pulled back by reflection, so this calculation holds for distributions. background_notes.justification: Repeated integration by parts gives Fourier decay faster than any fixed power for smooth periodic data. For m>r+1/2, Cauchy-Schwarz bounds sum_k |k|^r |hat f(k)| by a finite constant times ||f||H^m, yielding uniform convergence and continuity of r spatial derivatives, also continuously in time. The equation expresses U_t as a polynomial in spatial derivatives, continuous in all lower Sobolev orders; a continuous distributional time derivative integrates to a classical time derivative. Differentiating this polynomial identity repeatedly, using arbitrarily high spatial regularity, proves all mixed time and space derivatives continuous.
